behavior_items: The provided bug report title, "Type parameter inquiries for substrings are rejected", indicates the reproducer targets GCC Fortran front-end handling of substring expressions when they are used as the subject of a type-parameter inquiry.

In Fortran, a type-parameter inquiry accesses properties such as the length of a character entity, commonly through expressions like LEN(x) or the %len inquiry form on a character entity. The bug title implies the inquiry is being applied not to a whole character variable, but to a substring view such as x(i:j).

A substring expression is still character-valued and has a well-defined length derived from its bounds. Therefore, semantic analysis should accept length-related type inquiries on such expressions, either by directly computing the resulting substring length or by treating the substring as a valid character expression for inquiry purposes.

The reported failure mode is rejection by the compiler rather than incorrect runtime behavior. That means the reproducer exercises front-end parsing and semantic validation logic, specifically the rules that decide whether a given expression is a valid target of a type-parameter inquiry.

The likely compiler path being tested is one where GCC distinguishes between named variables/components and derived expressions. The bug suggests substring nodes were incorrectly excluded from the set of expressions considered valid for type-parameter inquiry, even though they should be accepted under the language rules.

If the reproducer is minimal, it probably declares a CHARACTER entity, forms a substring from it, and then performs a length inquiry in a context that requires compile-time or ordinary semantic acceptance. The expected result is successful compilation, because the substring length is determinable from the expression.

The bug therefore reflects an overly restrictive validity check in GCC's Fortran front end: it recognizes inquiries on full character entities, but rejects equivalent inquiries when the entity is wrapped in substring syntax.

This is a compile-time conformance issue. The reproducer is not mainly about execution semantics, optimization, or code generation; it is about whether the compiler correctly models substring expressions as legitimate character expressions with queryable type parameters.

Because only the bug title and not the concrete source code are provided, the exact syntax path cannot be enumerated. However, the exercised behavior is clear: a legal Fortran character substring expression is subjected to a type-parameter inquiry, and GCC erroneously diagnoses it as invalid.

The expected correct compiler behavior is to accept the program and evaluate the inquiry according to substring semantics, with the substring's character length derived from its slice bounds and base character object.
test_behavior_analysis.summary: The reproducer for GCC bug 101735 targets a Fortran front-end semantic bug involving character substrings. A substring expression such as x(i:j) remains a valid character expression with a well-defined length, so a type-parameter inquiry on it should be accepted. GCC instead rejects that inquiry during semantic checking, implying its validation logic incorrectly disallows substring expression nodes as inquiry operands. The reproducer therefore exercises compile-time language conformance for character type-parameter inquiries, not runtime execution or optimization behavior.

test_failure_analysis.analysis: The failure pattern points to a Fortran front-end semantic validation bug, not a runtime or code-generation issue. The common pattern is that the compiler accepts type-parameter inquiries on ordinary CHARACTER entities but rejects the same inquiry when the operand is a substring expression. Since a substring remains a valid character-valued expression with a well-defined derived length, rejection indicates GCC likely classifies substring parse/semantic nodes too narrowly during inquiry checking. The bug is therefore most consistent with an overly restrictive front-end rule that only permits inquiry on variables, components, or full designators, while failing to recognize substring references as legal character inquiry operands. A related possibility is that the substring node loses or fails to propagate character type-parameter metadata, causing later semantic checks to conclude that no valid length parameter exists. Overall, the likely defect lies in Fortran expression resolution or inquiry validation logic for substring expressions.

Given a completely parsed select statement, we: - Validate all expressions and code within the SELECT. - Make sure that the selection expression is not of the wrong type. - Make sure that no case ranges overlap. - Eliminate unreachable cases and unreachable code resulting from removing case labels. The standard does allow unreachable cases, e.g. CASE (5:3). But they are a hassle for code generation, and to prevent that, we just cut them out here. This is not necessary for overlapping cases because they are illegal and we never even try to generate code. We have the additional caveat that a SELECT construct could have been a computed GOTO in the source code. Fortunately we can fairly easily work around that here: The case_expr for a "real" SELECT CASE is in code->expr1, but for a computed GOTO it is in code->expr2. We store accesses in one of the two lists: PBEFORE_SP, and PNO_SP. If this expression or its only operand forces a sequence point, then everything up to the sequence point is stored in PBEFORE_SP. Everything else gets stored in PNO_SP. Once we return, we will have emitted warnings if any subexpression before such a sequence point could be undefined. On a higher level, however, the sequence point may not be relevant, and we'll merge the two lists. Example: (b++, a) + b; The call that processes the COMPOUND_EXPR will store the increment of B in PBEFORE_SP, and the use of A in PNO_SP. The higher-level call that processes the PLUS_EXPR will need to merge the two lists so that eventually, all accesses end up on the same list (and we'll warn about the unordered subexpressions b++ and b. A note on merging. If we modify the former example so that our expression becomes (b++, b) + a care must be taken not simply to add all three expressions into the final PNO_SP list. The function merge_tlist takes care of that by merging the before-SP list of the COMPOUND_EXPR into its after-SP list

gcc/c/c-decl.cc.signature: static tree get_parm_array_spec (const struct c_parm *parm, tree attrs)
gcc/c/c-decl.cc.summary: Return attribute "arg spec" corresponding to an array/VLA parameter described by PARM, concatenated onto attributes ATTRS. The spec consists of one dollar symbol for each specified variable bound, one asterisk for each unspecified variable bound, followed by at most one specification of the most significant bound of an ordinary array parameter. For ordinary arrays the specification is either the constant bound itself, or the space character for an array with an unspecified bound (the [] form). Finally, a chain of specified variable bounds is appended to the spec, starting with the most significant bound. For example, the PARM T a[2][m][3][n] will produce __attribute__((arg spec ("[$$2]", m, n)). For T a typedef for an array with variable bounds, the bounds are included in the specification in the expected order. No "arg spec" is created for parameters of pointer types, making a distinction between T(*)[N] (or, equivalently, T[][N]) and the T[M][N] form, all of which have the same type and are represented the same, but only the last of which gets an "arg spec" describing the most significant bound M.
